AC Repair in Houston: What Your System Is Telling You

Air conditioner quit, short cycling, or blowing air that is barely cool? Sort out the symptom here, do the safe checks, then call the free line any hour to reach an independent Houston-area HVAC company.

Call (832) 662-4107 Match your symptom
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. AC Repair

When you need AC repair in Houston, the first job is figuring out what kind of failure you have. A system that will not start, one that runs but cannot keep up, and one that is leaking water are three very different problems. This page helps you narrow it down, do the checks that are safe for a homeowner, and know what a proper diagnostic visit should include before you pay for one.

Houston Air & Heating is not a contractor. It is a free phone line answered at any hour by an automated assistant. You say what the system is doing and which part of the Houston area you are in, and the assistant hands the call to an HVAC company that is independent and locally owned. That business sends the technician, prices the repair and bills you directly.

Why Houston air conditioners break when they do

The cooling season here is long and it does not let up. Under the 1991 to 2020 climate normals, the normal daily high at Bush Intercontinental sits in the low to mid 90s through most of June, July and August. Actual summers often run hotter than the averages: the National Weather Service Houston/Galveston office counted 145 days at or above 90 degrees in 2025, beating the old record of 142 set in 2011.

That means months of near continuous run time, and Gulf Coast humidity adds a second load: the system has to pull water out of the air, not just heat. The U.S. Department of Energy notes that electrical controls can fail from frequent on and off cycling and from corroded wires and terminals. Drain lines carry water every day for months. When something gives out, it is usually one worn part that finally failed under load.

One thing that is not a breakdown: on the hottest late afternoons a healthy system may fall a degree or two behind the thermostat, then catch up after sunset. If the air from the vents feels clearly cold and the house recovers overnight, that is usually normal for a Houston August.

Houston AC repair triage: symptom, likely cause, safe check

Use this table to describe the problem accurately when you call. It does not replace a diagnosis: only a technician with meters and gauges on your equipment can confirm which part failed.

Air conditioning symptoms, what they often point to, what a homeowner can safely check, and what a technician tests
What you noticeOften points toSafe check for youWhat a technician tests
House is warm, vents blow mild airChoked filter, iced indoor coil, outdoor fan stopped, refrigerant leakThermostat on Cool and below room temperature; look at the filterAirflow, then fan and compressor operation, then the refrigerant charge
Thermostat calls for cooling, nothing happensTripped breaker, dead thermostat batteries, drain safety switch, control faultFresh batteries; reset a tripped breaker one time onlyPower at both units, low voltage controls, the float switch
Outdoor unit hums, fan blade sits stillFailed start component or fan motor, compressor strugglingTurn the system off and leave it offElectrical components against their ratings, motor and compressor draw
Frost or ice on the copper linePoor airflow or low refrigerantSystem off, fan on, let it thaw; replace a dirty filterBlower and coil after thawing, then pressures and temperatures
Water at the indoor unit or a ceiling stainBlocked condensate drain, cracked pan, failed float switchSystem off, towels and a bucket downDrain cleared and flowing, pan condition, safety switch
Short on and off cycles all dayThermostat placement, electrical wear, charge problem, oversized equipmentMake sure the thermostat is not in sun or near a lampCycle timing, controls, charge, equipment sizing
Breaker trips again after one resetElectrical short in a motor, compressor or wiringLeave the breaker off and callInsulation and amperage tests before anything restarts

Safe checks a homeowner can do

Some no-cooling calls end with something simple. These steps never involve removing a panel, touching wires or handling refrigerant.

  1. Read the thermostat. Mode on Cool, set a few degrees below the room, fan on Auto. A blank screen often just needs new batteries.
  2. Pull the filter. If you cannot see light through it, put in a new one. A clogged filter cuts airflow, and the Department of Energy lists dirty filters among the most common causes of poor cooling.
  3. Check the breakers. The indoor and outdoor units usually have separate breakers. If one has tripped, you may flip it back on a single time. If it flips off again, stop there: repeat trips mean an electrical fault.
  4. Look at the outdoor unit. Clear leaves, grass clippings and overgrown plants from around it without reaching inside. Note whether the top fan spins when the system is calling for cooling.
  5. Look at the indoor unit. Standing water in the pan or a float switch that has tripped can shut the whole system down on purpose. Note it for the technician.

Still warm after those checks? Call and describe exactly what you saw: the thermostat reading, whether the outdoor fan turns, any ice or water. That summary goes to the company you are put through to.

What a good diagnostic visit looks like

A diagnostic visit is the technician's time spent finding the cause. You are paying for measurements, not a guess. A careful technician usually works in this order and tells you what the readings were.

  1. Ask you what happened. When it started, what you noticed, what you already checked. Your notes save time.
  2. Confirm airflow. Filter, blower, indoor coil and return air. Refrigerant readings mean little if the system is starved for air.
  3. Test the electrical side. Components measured against their rated values, motors and compressor checked for proper current draw.
  4. Measure the refrigerant side. Gauge pressures and pipe temperatures checked against the maker's charging data. A low charge always means refrigerant escaped somewhere, so the leak has to be located. Only a technician certified under EPA Section 608 may connect gauges or add refrigerant.
  5. Check the drain. The condensate line flushed and flowing and any float switch tested, which matters a lot in Houston homes with the air handler in the attic.
  6. Explain and price. What failed, why, what fixing it costs in writing, and anything else worth watching.

How long the repair itself takes

Many common fixes happen during the first visit if the part is on hand: a worn electrical component, a cleared drain, a replaced thermostat. A leak search can take longer because the technician has to trace the circuit. Big components, such as an indoor coil or a compressor, may need to be ordered and often take a separate trip. Attic work in summer is slow, hot work and can stretch the clock.

If you are told the part is days away, ask whether anything can get partial cooling going in the meantime, and whether the price changes if it arrives sooner.

Before you approve the repair, ask

  • What is the visit or diagnostic fee?Get the number before anyone is dispatched, and ask whether it counts toward the repair.
  • What is your Texas ACR license number?Texas requires an ACR contractor license, issued by TDLR, for this kind of work. Look the number up yourself.
  • What did you measure?A technician who tested something can tell you the reading and show you the failed part.
  • Can I have the total in writing?Parts, labor and refrigerant, before the work begins.
  • If refrigerant is low, where is the leak?The EPA advises asking for leaks to be found and repaired rather than having a leaking system topped off.
  • Is this worth repairing at this age?If replacement comes up, ask for the repair price too. The repair or replace guide walks through the decision.

Verify the license before work begins. Texas requires anyone contracting to do air conditioning, refrigeration or heating work to hold an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration (ACR) Contractor license from the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). Ask the company for its ACR license number, then confirm it on the TDLR license search (opens in a new tab). The line does not check this for you.

For a closer look at how individual parts fail and what each repair involves, see the air conditioning repair guide to components. If the problem is a system that runs but will not cool, the AC not cooling guide goes deeper, and for drips and puddles there is the AC leaking water guide.

Fewer repair calls next summer

Change the filter on schedule through the cooling season. Keep shrubs, mulch and mower clippings away from the outdoor unit. Pick a steady setting: ENERGY STAR's thermostat guidance uses 78 degrees for the hours you are home in summer, and setting the thermostat far lower does not cool the house faster, it only keeps the system running longer. A spring HVAC tune-up, before the first heat wave, gives a technician time to catch a worn part while it is still a small job.

Common questions

How long does AC repair take?

It depends on what failed and whether the part is on the truck. Small electrical parts and a clogged condensate drain are often handled during the first visit once the problem is found. A refrigerant leak that has to be located, an indoor coil, a compressor, or any part that has to be ordered takes longer, sometimes several days. Ask the technician for an honest timeline before you approve the work.

Can I get AC repair today in Houston?

The phone line picks up at any hour and puts you through to a local, independently owned HVAC business. Whether a technician gets to you today depends on that business's schedule and how busy the season is. Before you hang up, ask for a likely arrival window and the visit fee.

Is Houston Air and Heating an AC repair company?

No. Houston Air and Heating only answers the phone for free and passes your call to a separate, locally owned heating and cooling business. That business sends a technician, sets the price and collects payment from you. It may pay the line a referral fee.

Should I keep running my AC if it is blowing warm air?

Do the quick checks first: thermostat on Cool, a clean filter, breakers on. If the air is still warm, or you see ice on the copper line, hear humming with no fan turning, or smell burning, switch the system off at the thermostat. Running a struggling system can turn a small repair into a compressor replacement.

How much does AC repair cost in Houston?

Prices come from the company doing the work, never from the line. The cost depends on the failed part, labor, how hard the equipment is to reach, refrigerant if a leak is involved, and whether the visit is after hours. The AC repair cost guide explains published ranges and what drives them. Always get the diagnostic fee and a written repair price before work starts.
